prompt: Ultrasound is defined as sound with frequency

options.text: Greater than 20 kHz (above human hearing)
Less than 20 Hz (below human hearing)
Between 20 Hz and 20 kHz (audible range)
Greater than 2 MHz (the diagnostic range)

explanation: Ultrasound is sound above 20 kHz, beyond human hearing. Diagnostic imaging typically uses 2–15 MHz; that MHz range is a subset of ultrasound, not the definition.

distractorExplanations.b: Sound below 20 Hz is infrasound; ultrasound is the opposite end, above the upper limit of hearing.
distractorExplanations.c: 20 Hz to 20 kHz is audible sound; ultrasound begins above 20 kHz.
distractorExplanations.d: About 2 MHz is the low end of typical diagnostic imaging; the definition of ultrasound starts at 20 kHz.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Wavelength equals

options.text: Propagation speed times frequency (c × f)
Spatial pulse length times number of cycles
Frequency divided by propagation speed (f/c)
Propagation speed divided by frequency (c/f)

explanation: λ = c/f; higher frequency → shorter wavelength → better axial resolution generally.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplying speed by frequency gives the wrong units; wavelength is speed divided by frequency (λ = c/f).
distractorExplanations.b: SPL equals cycles × wavelength, so wavelength is SPL divided by the number of cycles, not multiplied by it.
distractorExplanations.c: That inverts the ratio; f/c equals 1/λ, so higher frequency would wrongly give a longer wavelength.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Propagation speed is determined primarily by:

options.text: The transducer's operating frequency
The amplitude and intensity of the pulse
Medium stiffness (elasticity) and density
Pulse repetition frequency and depth setting

explanation: Soft tissue average ~1540 m/s; stiffer media generally faster sound.

distractorExplanations.a: Frequency is set by the source; speed is a property of the medium and is the same for all frequencies in soft tissue.
distractorExplanations.b: Amplitude and intensity describe the strength of the wave; they do not change how fast sound travels in a medium.
distractorExplanations.d: PRF and depth control pulse timing on the machine; the medium's stiffness and density set propagation speed.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Acoustic impedance (Z) equals

options.text: Frequency × wavelength
Density divided by propagation speed
Stiffness × propagation speed
Density × propagation speed

explanation: Acoustic impedance Z = density × propagation speed. Large Z mismatches (soft tissue–air, soft tissue–bone) reflect strongly; similar Z values transmit.

distractorExplanations.a: Frequency times wavelength equals speed (c = fλ), not acoustic impedance Z = ρc.
distractorExplanations.b: Density divided by speed is not a used ultrasound quantity; Z is density times speed.
distractorExplanations.c: Frequency times density is not impedance; Z does not include frequency.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Period and frequency are

options.text: Set by the medium
Directly proportional (T ∝ f)
Reciprocals (T = 1/f)
Related by the speed (T = c/f)

explanation: Source (transducer) determines frequency/period; medium determines speed.

distractorExplanations.a: The sound source (transducer) sets both period and frequency; the medium sets propagation speed.
distractorExplanations.b: As frequency rises the period gets shorter, so the two are inversely related, not directly proportional.
distractorExplanations.d: Speed divided by frequency gives wavelength (λ = c/f); period is simply the reciprocal of frequency.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Power is proportional to amplitude

options.text: Cubed always
Squared (≈ A^2)
To the zeroth power
Inversely

explanation: Power and intensity both vary with amplitude squared. Doubling amplitude quadruples intensity, which is why output and bioeffect discussions track amplitude carefully.

distractorExplanations.a: The relation is amplitude squared, not linear in amplitude; doubling amplitude quadruples power.
distractorExplanations.c: Power is not independent of amplitude; it scales with amplitude squared.
distractorExplanations.d: Power is not inversely proportional to amplitude; higher amplitude means higher power.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Attenuation in soft tissue increases when:

options.text: Frequency decreases with path fixed always reducing attenuation
You freeze the image
Path length or frequency increases
Gain is increased (true attenuation change)

explanation: Attenuation coefficient rises with frequency; more depth → more loss.

distractorExplanations.a: Lower f penetrates better.
distractorExplanations.b: Freeze doesn't change physics.
distractorExplanations.d: Gain amplifies display, not true attenuation.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: The decibel (dB) scale for intensity ratios is

options.text: Linear: 3 dB ≈ factor of 3; 10 dB ≈ factor of 10
Logarithmic: 3 dB ≈ factor of 2; 10 dB ≈ factor of 100
An absolute unit of intensity in W/cm²
Logarithmic: 3 dB ≈ factor of 2; 10 dB ≈ factor of 10

explanation: Know common dB doublings for intensity/amplitude conventions taught in SPI.

distractorExplanations.a: The dB scale is logarithmic, not linear; +3 dB doubles intensity rather than tripling it.
distractorExplanations.b: 3 dB does double intensity, but 10 dB is a factor of 10; a factor of 100 is 20 dB.
distractorExplanations.c: Decibels express a relative ratio; W/cm² is the absolute unit of intensity, not the dB scale.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Specular reflection occurs when:

options.text: The interface is large and smooth relative to wavelength
Scatterers are much smaller than wavelength only (Rayleigh)
The interface is rough and irregular relative to wavelength
Impedances on both sides of the boundary are equal

explanation: Specular reflections are angle-dependent; diffuse scattering from rough surfaces.

distractorExplanations.b: Rayleigh is small scatterers.
distractorExplanations.c: Rough, irregular interfaces cause diffuse scattering (backscatter) in many directions, not specular reflection.
distractorExplanations.d: With equal impedances there is no mismatch, so no reflection of any kind occurs at the boundary.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Snell's law relates to:

options.text: Reflection—the angle of reflection equals incidence
Refraction—bending of the beam across an oblique interface
Attenuation—loss of beam intensity with depth and frequency
Scattering—redirection of sound by small reflectors

explanation: Refraction can laterally displace structures (e.g., edge artifacts/duodenum-type teaching cases); it bends the beam when speed changes across an oblique interface.

distractorExplanations.a: Equal angles of incidence and reflection is the law of reflection; Snell's law governs the transmitted (refracted) beam.
distractorExplanations.c: Attenuation describes energy loss with depth and frequency; Snell's law describes the change in beam direction.
distractorExplanations.d: Scattering from small or rough reflectors is not described by Snell's law, which relates angles to speed ratios.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Intensity of an ultrasound beam is proportional to:

options.text: Amplitude squared
Amplitude cubed
Wavelength squared
Square root of power

explanation: Acoustic intensity relates to amplitude squared (power/area considerations) for a given medium relationship.

distractorExplanations.b: Intensity scales with the square of amplitude, so doubling amplitude quadruples intensity, not an eightfold rise.
distractorExplanations.c: Wavelength affects resolution and attenuation; intensity depends on amplitude squared, not wavelength.
distractorExplanations.d: Intensity is power divided by beam area, so it is directly proportional to power, not to its square root.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Refraction occurs when a sound beam

options.text: Hits a boundary at 90° between media with different speeds
Obliquely encounters media with different propagation speeds
Obliquely meets media with different impedances but equal speeds
Passes through a single uniform medium at a steady speed

explanation: Snell's law: refraction needs oblique incidence and speed mismatch.

distractorExplanations.a: At normal (90°) incidence there is no refraction even when speeds differ; obliquity is required.
distractorExplanations.c: An impedance mismatch alone causes reflection; refraction requires a difference in propagation speeds.
distractorExplanations.d: With no boundary and no speed change there is nothing to bend the beam, so refraction cannot occur.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Pulse repetition frequency (PRF) is

options.text: The number of pulses transmitted per second
The time from the start of one pulse to the end of that pulse
Always equal to operating frequency
Unrelated to imaging depth

explanation: PRF is the number of pulses sent per second. Deeper imaging needs a longer listening time, so PRF must fall to avoid range ambiguity.

distractorExplanations.b: Pulse duration is the time one pulse is on, not how many pulses are sent each second.
distractorExplanations.c: Duty factor is the on-time fraction (PD × PRF), not the pulse rate itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Period is the time of one cycle inside a pulse, not the number of pulses per second.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Increasing imaging depth while keeping other factors constant typically requires:

options.text: Higher PRF
Lower PRF to allow time for echoes to return
Shorter listening time
Elimination of the range equation

explanation: Echoes from greater depth take longer to return. To wait for those echoes before the next pulse, PRF (and often frame rate) must decrease, or range-ambiguity artifact appears.

distractorExplanations.a: Raising PRF at greater depth invites range ambiguity because the next pulse is sent before late echoes arrive.
distractorExplanations.c: Wavelength is set by frequency and speed, not by imaging depth.
distractorExplanations.d: Increasing depth does not raise duty factor by itself; the system usually drops PRF instead.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1).

prompt: Decibels (dB) in ultrasound describe

options.text: Absolute beam intensity measured in watts per square centimeter
Relative changes in intensity or amplitude on a logarithmic scale
Changes in pulse frequency expressed on a linear kilohertz scale
The depth of a reflector calculated from echo return time

explanation: dB express ratios (e.g., attenuation, gain changes) logarithmically.

distractorExplanations.a: W/cm² is the absolute unit of intensity; decibels express relative ratios, not absolute values.
distractorExplanations.c: Frequency is measured in hertz; decibels are logarithmic ratios of intensity or amplitude, not frequency.
distractorExplanations.d: Reflector depth comes from the range equation (13 µs per cm round trip), not from decibel measurements.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Piezoelectric effect means:

options.text: Magnetic fields make the crystal change shape to emit sound
Electric current heats a crystal, which then emits sound
Certain materials convert pressure to electricity and vice versa
Materials convert electricity to pressure but not the reverse

explanation: PZT elements transmit and receive; Curie temperature destroys piezoelectricity if overheated.

distractorExplanations.a: Shape change driven by a magnetic field is magnetostriction, not the piezoelectric effect, which uses voltage.
distractorExplanations.b: Heating does not produce the ultrasound pulse; voltage deforms the crystal directly, and heat can destroy it above the Curie point.
distractorExplanations.d: The effect is reciprocal: the same element converts voltage to pressure on transmit and pressure to voltage on receive.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Matching layer function is to:

options.text: Shorten the pulse by absorbing the crystal's ringing
Raise the impedance above that of PZT
Focus the beam in the elevation plane
Improve transmission between PZT and tissue

explanation: The matching layer has an impedance between PZT and tissue, improving transmission; its thickness is about 1/4 wavelength.

distractorExplanations.a: Absorbing ringing to shorten the pulse is the job of the backing (damping) material behind the crystal.
distractorExplanations.b: The matching layer impedance sits between PZT and skin; raising it above PZT would increase reflection.
distractorExplanations.c: Elevational focusing is done by the acoustic lens, not by the matching layer.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Backing/damping material mainly

options.text: Increases ringing to raise the quality factor (Q)
Improves lateral resolution by narrowing the beam width
Shortens spatial pulse length improving axial resolution
Increases sensitivity by lengthening the transmitted pulse

explanation: Low-Q damped transducers are used for imaging; continuous wave Doppler is lightly damped. Damping shortens SPL at the cost of sensitivity.

distractorExplanations.a: Damping reduces ringing and lowers Q (wider bandwidth); higher Q belongs to lightly damped CW transducers.
distractorExplanations.b: Beam width and lateral resolution are improved by focusing, not by the backing material.
distractorExplanations.d: Damping shortens the pulse and actually reduces sensitivity; it does not lengthen the pulse.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Axial resolution improves with:

options.text: Narrower beam width at the focus
Lower transducer frequency
More cycles in the pulse
Shorter spatial pulse length

explanation: AR ≈ SPL/2; fewer cycles and shorter λ help, so higher frequency and more damping improve axial resolution.

distractorExplanations.a: Beam width governs lateral resolution; axial resolution depends on spatial pulse length.
distractorExplanations.b: Lower frequency means longer wavelength and longer SPL, which worsens axial resolution.
distractorExplanations.c: More cycles lengthen SPL.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Lateral resolution is best at the

options.text: Transducer face, near the crystal
Far (Fraunhofer) zone
Focus (narrowest beam width)
Deepest part of the image

explanation: Focusing improves lateral resolution at the focal zone; multiple foci reduce frame rate.

distractorExplanations.a: At the face the beam is as wide as the crystal, about twice its width at the focus.
distractorExplanations.b: The beam diverges in the far zone, so lateral resolution degrades beyond the focus.
distractorExplanations.d: The deepest region is in the diverging far field, where beam width and lateral resolution are worst.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Linear sequenced arrays create rectangular images by:

options.text: Steering one beam with phased delays from all elements
Firing groups of elements in sequence across the face
Rotating a single element with a motor inside the probe
Firing every element together as one large crystal

explanation: Linear = rectangle; convex = blunted sector; phased = sector from small footprint.

distractorExplanations.a: Steering with phased time delays from a small footprint produces a sector image, which is a phased array.
distractorExplanations.c: A motor-driven single element is an older mechanical sector transducer, not a linear sequenced array.
distractorExplanations.d: Firing all elements at once makes one wide unsteered beam; linear arrays build lines by firing small groups in turn.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Phased array steering uses

options.text: A motor that rotates a single crystal
Firing element groups in sequence along the face
Minute time delays (phasing) across elements
A curved face that spreads the scan lines

explanation: Electronic beam forming with minute time delays steers/focuses the beam, enabling sector imaging from small probes (cardiac).

distractorExplanations.a: A rotating crystal describes a mechanical sector transducer; phased arrays steer electronically.
distractorExplanations.b: Sequential firing of element groups is how linear sequenced arrays make rectangular images.
distractorExplanations.d: A curved face produces the blunted sector of a convex array; phased arrays steer with timing delays.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Grating lobes are reduced by:

options.text: Increasing output power and overall receiver gain
Wider element spacing across a larger total aperture
Lowering the frame rate with more transmit foci
Apodization, subdicing, and tight element spacing

explanation: Grating/side lobes create artifacts and degrade lateral resolution.

distractorExplanations.a: More power and gain raise lobe energy along with the main beam; they do not suppress grating lobes.
distractorExplanations.b: Wider element spacing makes grating lobes worse; elements should be spaced closely (about half a wavelength).
distractorExplanations.c: More transmit foci improve lateral resolution across depth but do not address grating lobes.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Duty factor is

options.text: Pulse duration divided by pulse repetition period
Pulse repetition period divided by the pulse duration
Pulse duration multiplied by the frame rate
Pulse duration divided by the wave period

explanation: DF is unitless (the fraction of time transmitting); CW Doppler DF = 1; imaging DF is very small.

distractorExplanations.b: That inverts the ratio and would give values above 1; duty factor is PD/PRP, a fraction of time transmitting.
distractorExplanations.c: Frame rate is not the pulse repetition frequency; duty factor uses PD × PRF (equivalently PD/PRP).
distractorExplanations.d: Pulse duration divided by the wave period gives the number of cycles in the pulse, not duty factor.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Spatial pulse length equals

options.text: Number of cycles × period
Number of cycles × wavelength
Wavelength ÷ number of cycles
Propagation speed ÷ frequency (c/f)

explanation: Spatial pulse length = number of cycles × wavelength. Shorter SPL (damping, higher frequency) improves axial resolution. Cycles × period is pulse duration, a time, not a length.

distractorExplanations.a: Cycles multiplied by period gives pulse duration (a time), not spatial pulse length (a distance).
distractorExplanations.c: SPL grows with more cycles, so it is wavelength multiplied by cycles, not divided.
distractorExplanations.d: c/f equals one wavelength; SPL is that wavelength multiplied by the number of cycles in the pulse.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: The piezoelectric effect describes:

options.text: Conversion between electrical energy and mechanical energy
Conversion of electrical energy into heat within the crystal
Conversion between light and sound energy in crystals
Conversion of magnetic energy into sound in the probe

explanation: Piezoelectric materials expand/contract with voltage and generate voltage from pressure, converting between electrical and mechanical (sound) energy in crystals.

distractorExplanations.b: Heat is an unwanted by-product; the piezoelectric effect converts voltage into mechanical vibration and back.
distractorExplanations.c: Light-to-sound conversion is the photoacoustic effect, not piezoelectricity.
distractorExplanations.d: Magnetic-to-mechanical conversion is magnetostriction; piezoelectric crystals respond to voltage.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Increasing the number of transmit foci typically

options.text: Improves lateral resolution at multiple depths but can reduce frame rate
Improves lateral resolution at multiple depths and raises frame rate
Improves axial resolution at multiple depths but reduces frame rate
Reduces frame rate without changing lateral resolution

explanation: Multiple foci improve lateral resolution over depth at a temporal-resolution cost.

distractorExplanations.b: Each extra focus needs another transmit pulse per line, so frame rate falls rather than rises.
distractorExplanations.c: Focusing narrows beam width, which affects lateral resolution; axial resolution depends on SPL.
distractorExplanations.d: Frame rate does fall, but the purpose and effect of extra foci is better lateral resolution over depth.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Axial resolution is approximately equal to

options.text: One-half of the spatial pulse length
The number of cycles in the pulse times the period
Pulse duration times pulse repetition frequency
Twice the spatial pulse length

explanation: Axial (longitudinal) resolution ≈ SPL/2. Shorter spatial pulse length — fewer cycles or shorter wavelength — improves the ability to separate two reflectors along the beam. Pulse duration × PRF is duty factor, not resolution.

distractorExplanations.b: Cycles times period is pulse duration (time), not a spatial resolution length.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulse duration times PRF equals duty factor, the fraction of time the system is transmitting.
distractorExplanations.d: Doubling SPL would worsen axial resolution; the formula is SPL/2, not 2×SPL.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: A convex (curved) array produces an image that is typically

options.text: A pie-shaped sector that converges to a tiny footprint
Blunted-sector shaped with a wider field at depth
Rectangular with a constant width at depth
Trapezoidal from steering a flat linear face

explanation: Curved arrays create blunted sector formats common in abdominal imaging, from sequential firing along a curved face.

distractorExplanations.a: A pointed sector from a small footprint is the phased-array format; convex arrays have a broad curved top.
distractorExplanations.c: A rectangle of constant width is produced by a linear sequenced array, not a curved array.
distractorExplanations.d: A trapezoid comes from steering the outer lines of a flat linear array (virtual convex), not a curved face.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local QA repair (stems/distractors)

prompt: Bandwidth of a transducer relates to:

options.text: The range of frequencies in the pulse
The main (resonant) frequency of the crystal
The number of pulses sent per second
The width of the beam at the focus

explanation: Bandwidth is the range of frequencies in the transmitted/received pulse; broader bandwidth (more damping) shortens pulses and improves axial resolution.

distractorExplanations.b: The resonant frequency is the center or operating frequency; bandwidth is the spread of frequencies around it.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulses per second is the pulse repetition frequency, a timing setting unrelated to bandwidth.
distractorExplanations.d: Beam width at the focus governs lateral resolution; bandwidth is a frequency range, not a dimension.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: The Doppler shift is proportional to:

options.text: Reflector speed, the cosine of the Doppler angle, and operating frequency
Reflector speed, the sine of the Doppler angle, and operating frequency
Reflector speed and operating frequency, but not the Doppler angle
The pulse repetition frequency and the depth of the sample gate

explanation: Doppler shift fd = 2 v f0 cosθ / c. Shift rises with flow speed and operating frequency and falls as the beam–flow angle approaches 90°.

distractorExplanations.b: The Doppler equation uses cosine, which is maximal at 0°; sine would wrongly make the shift maximal at 90°.
distractorExplanations.c: The shift depends on cos θ, so the angle matters and must be corrected for velocity estimates.
distractorExplanations.d: PRF and gate depth set the Nyquist limit and range, not the magnitude of the Doppler shift itself.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: At a Doppler angle of 90°

options.text: Cosine is 1 so the Doppler shift is maximal
Velocity estimates are at their most accurate
Cosine is 0.5 so the shift is halved
Cosine is 0 so no Doppler shift is detected

explanation: Avoid 90°; aim for ≤60° for quantitative vascular Doppler when possible.

distractorExplanations.a: Cos θ equals 1 at 0°, where the shift is maximal; at 90° cosine is 0.
distractorExplanations.b: Angles near 90° give the largest velocity errors; keep the angle at or below 60° for velocity estimates.
distractorExplanations.c: Cos θ equals 0.5 at 60°; at 90° it is 0 and no shift is detected.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Aliasing in pulsed Doppler occurs when:

options.text: The wall filter is set too high for slow flow
CW Doppler is used (CW aliases the same way)
Nyquist limit is exceeded (shift > PRF/2)
The Doppler shift is below PRF/2

explanation: Fix aliasing by increasing PRF/scale, adjusting baseline, lower f0, shallower sample, or switch to CW.

distractorExplanations.a: A high wall filter removes low-velocity signals near the baseline; it does not cause wraparound aliasing.
distractorExplanations.b: CW does not alias the same (no PRF sampling limit).
distractorExplanations.d: A shift below PRF/2 is under the Nyquist limit and is displayed correctly; aliasing needs a shift above it.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Continuous-wave Doppler advantage is

options.text: Precise depth range resolution of the source of shift
No need for two crystals/elements concepts
Immunity to any angle effects
Ability to measure high velocities without aliasing

explanation: Continuous-wave Doppler has no pulse listening window, so it measures high velocities without aliasing, but it cannot select a depth (range ambiguity along the entire beam). Pulsed-wave Doppler has a sample volume and can alias.

distractorExplanations.a: CW cannot isolate depth; that range resolution is the PW advantage.
distractorExplanations.b: CW probes typically use two elements (one send, one receive); that is a construction fact, not the clinical advantage.
distractorExplanations.c: Angle still affects CW velocity estimates; cosine θ remains in the Doppler equation.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Bernoulli equation simplified in echo estimates pressure gradients from:

options.text: v^2/4 (velocity squared over 4)
4v (peak velocity × 4)
4v^2 (modified Bernoulli)
8v^2 (doubled for valves)

explanation: ΔP ≈ 4v² relates peak velocity to pressure drop across stenoses/valves.

distractorExplanations.a: The factor 4 multiplies v², it does not divide it; ΔP = 4v² in mmHg with v in m/s.
distractorExplanations.b: The velocity must be squared; ΔP = 4v², so 4 m/s gives 64 mmHg, not 16 mmHg.
distractorExplanations.d: The simplified constant is 4, not 8; there is no doubling for valves in the modified Bernoulli equation.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1).

prompt: Reynolds number predicts

options.text: Pressure drop across a stenotic valve
Tendency for laminar vs turbulent flow
Volume flow rate through a vessel
Maximum velocity before aliasing occurs

explanation: High Reynolds (high velocity, large diameter, low viscosity) → turbulence; spectral window fill-in.

distractorExplanations.a: Pressure drop across a stenosis is estimated with the Bernoulli equation, not the Reynolds number.
distractorExplanations.c: Volume flow is described by Poiseuille's law (Q = ΔP/R), not by the Reynolds number.
distractorExplanations.d: The maximum unaliased velocity is set by the Nyquist limit (PRF/2), not by the Reynolds number.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Color Doppler packet size (ensemble length) tradeoff

options.text: Larger packets improve velocity estimates and raise frame rate
Smaller packets improve sensitivity but reduce frame rate
Larger packets improve velocity estimates but reduce frame rate
Larger packets reduce aliasing by raising the color Nyquist limit

explanation: Color is multi-pulse; compromises among area, depth, packets, and PRF.

distractorExplanations.a: Each extra pulse per line takes time, so larger packets lower the frame rate.
distractorExplanations.b: Smaller packets raise frame rate but reduce sensitivity and velocity accuracy; the tradeoff is reversed.
distractorExplanations.d: The Nyquist limit depends on PRF, not packet size; larger packets do not reduce aliasing.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Wall filters (high-pass) remove

options.text: Only the highest arterial velocities always as their purpose
ECG signals in the ultrasound machine power cord
All useful diastolic venous flow by design goal when set optimally
Low-frequency Doppler shifts from vessel wall/clutter motion

explanation: Excessive wall filter can wipe out slow flow (e.g., venous/diastolic)

distractorExplanations.a: Not for removing peak arterial.
distractorExplanations.b: Not electrical ECG filtering definition.
distractorExplanations.c: Overfiltering harms slow flow.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Power Doppler displays

options.text: Peak velocity over time as a spectrum
Mean velocity and direction of flow
Strength/amplitude of Doppler shifts
Tissue motion rather than blood flow

explanation: Power Doppler displays signal strength rather than mean velocity/direction; it is more sensitive to flow presence and less angle dependent than color.

distractorExplanations.a: A velocity-time spectrum is the spectral Doppler display, not power Doppler.
distractorExplanations.b: Mean velocity and direction are what color (velocity) Doppler maps; power Doppler shows signal strength.
distractorExplanations.d: Low-velocity, high-amplitude tissue motion is displayed by tissue Doppler imaging, not power Doppler.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Spectral broadening may indicate

options.text: Plug flow sampled with a small gate volume
Turbulent flow or large sample volume
A Doppler angle of exactly 0°
Aliasing from too low a PRF

explanation: Fill-in of the spectral window suggests turbulence or technical factors, such as a large sample volume encompassing varied velocities.

distractorExplanations.a: Plug flow with a small gate has a narrow velocity range and a clear spectral window, the opposite of broadening.
distractorExplanations.c: A 0° angle maximizes the shift and minimizes geometric broadening; it does not cause spectral fill-in.
distractorExplanations.d: Aliasing wraps the peak velocities around the baseline; it does not fill in the spectral window.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: The Doppler equation shows Doppler shift increases when:

options.text: Reflector speed increases (toward/away component) or operating frequency increases, for a given angle factor
Propagation speed in tissue becomes infinite
The Doppler angle is exactly 90°
PRF is set to zero

explanation: From fd = 2 v f0 cosθ / c, Doppler shift increases when velocity or transmit frequency rises, or when the angle is closer to 0° (larger cosine). It falls at 90°.

distractorExplanations.b: A 90° angle makes cosθ ≈ 0, so the shift nearly disappears rather than increases.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher propagation speed in the denominator lowers the shift; it does not increase it.
distractorExplanations.d: A drop in operating frequency or a move toward 90° reduces the Doppler shift; the shift rises with speed and frequency at a given angle.

prompt: Power Doppler imaging is particularly useful because it

options.text: Shows flow direction and mean velocity more accurately than color Doppler
Is more sensitive to low flow and less angle-dependent than velocity color Doppler
Is less prone to flash artifact and has a higher frame rate than color Doppler
Measures peak velocities for stenosis grading without angle correction

explanation: Power Doppler encodes strength of the Doppler signal; it is relatively angle-insensitive compared with color velocity maps and does not show direction/velocity magnitude the same way.

distractorExplanations.a: Power Doppler does not display direction or velocity magnitude; that is the strength of color and spectral Doppler.
distractorExplanations.c: Power Doppler is more prone to flash (motion) artifact and usually has a lower frame rate than color Doppler.
distractorExplanations.d: Stenosis grading needs angle-corrected spectral velocities; power Doppler gives no velocity values.

prompt: Laminar flow is characterized by:

options.text: Chaotic multidirectional velocities filling the spectrum at rest
Streamlined layers with a relatively narrow range of velocities
Fastest layers at the walls and slowest layers in the center
Flow that reverses direction in every cardiac cycle

explanation: Laminar flow moves in parallel layers with a relatively narrow velocity range — fastest in the center of the vessel, slowest at the walls. Turbulent flow is chaotic with a wide velocity spectrum and often a bruit.

distractorExplanations.a: Plug flow is a blunt, nearly uniform profile at the entrance of a vessel; laminar (parabolic) flow has a range of layer speeds, fastest in the center.
distractorExplanations.c: In laminar (parabolic) flow the fastest layers are in the center and the slowest are at the walls — not the reverse.
distractorExplanations.d: Brief flow reversal can appear in triphasic arterial waveforms and still be laminar; reversal does not define laminar flow.

prompt: Sample volume (gate) size in pulsed Doppler affects

options.text: The Nyquist limit at any given depth
Which portion of the vessel is interrogated
The Doppler angle used for velocity correction
The transmitted frequency of the Doppler beam

explanation: Larger gates include more of the vessel and more velocity components, which can increase spectral broadening.

distractorExplanations.a: The Nyquist limit depends on PRF, which is set by gate depth, not by gate size.
distractorExplanations.c: The Doppler angle is set by beam steering and the angle cursor, not by the size of the sample gate.
distractorExplanations.d: The transmitted frequency is chosen on the transducer; gate size does not change it.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Autocorrelation in color Doppler is used to:

options.text: Estimate mean Doppler shifts rapidly across many gates
Display the full velocity spectrum at a single gate
Estimate peak Doppler shifts using fast Fourier transform
Suppress wall motion clutter from the color image

explanation: Color flow uses autocorrelation (or similar) for fast mean-velocity estimates across many gates for the color display.

distractorExplanations.b: Displaying the full spectrum at one gate is spectral Doppler, which uses FFT rather than autocorrelation.
distractorExplanations.c: FFT is the processing method for spectral Doppler; color Doppler uses autocorrelation to estimate mean shifts.
distractorExplanations.d: Clutter from wall motion is removed by the wall (clutter) filter, not by autocorrelation.

prompt: Shadowing artifact occurs distal to:

options.text: Areas where far-field TGC is set too high
Fluid-filled simple cysts and the bladder
Highly attenuating/reflecting structures
Tissues with lower propagation speed than 1540

explanation: Useful diagnostically for stones; distinguish from improper TGC. Shadows form deep to calcifications, stones and bone.

distractorExplanations.a: Excess far-field TGC makes deep tissue too bright; it does not create an acoustic shadow.
distractorExplanations.b: Low-attenuating fluid such as cysts and the bladder produces enhancement, the opposite of shadowing.
distractorExplanations.d: Speed differences cause range (depth) errors and refraction, not shadowing distal to a structure.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Acoustic enhancement is seen distal to:

options.text: Gallstones and renal calculi
Low-attenuating fluid (cysts, bladder)
Calcified arterial plaque
Dense solid masses that absorb most of the beam

explanation: Acoustic enhancement (through-transmission) appears distal to a low-attenuating structure such as a cyst. The beam is stronger than the TGC expects, so the tissue behind looks brighter.

distractorExplanations.a: Stones are highly attenuating and cast shadows, not enhancement.
distractorExplanations.c: Calcified plaque reflects and attenuates strongly, producing a shadow rather than enhancement.
distractorExplanations.d: Highly attenuating solid masses cause shadowing; enhancement occurs deep to low-attenuating fluid.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Reverberation artifact appears as:

options.text: A duplicate structure deep to a strong curved reflector
A structure displaced sideways at an oblique interface
Multiple equally spaced echoes at increasing depths
Dark bands distal to a highly attenuating structure

explanation: Reverberation produces multiple equally spaced echoes from strong parallel reflectors; comet-tail/ring-down are related variants taught in SPI.

distractorExplanations.a: A duplicate image deep to a strong curved reflector such as the diaphragm is mirror-image artifact.
distractorExplanations.b: Sideways displacement at an oblique interface is a refraction artifact.
distractorExplanations.d: Dark bands distal to an attenuating structure are acoustic shadowing, not reverberation.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Mirror image artifact commonly occurs around

options.text: Simple cysts with posterior enhancement
Small calcifications causing comet tails
Curved cyst edges that bend the beam
Strong reflectors like diaphragm/pleura

explanation: Strong reflectors like the diaphragm/pleura create a duplicated structure; liver lesions can appear mirrored into the lung base.

distractorExplanations.a: Posterior enhancement deep to cysts is a through-transmission artifact, not a mirror image.
distractorExplanations.b: Comet tails from small calcifications or metal are a reverberation artifact, not mirror image.
distractorExplanations.c: Beam bending at curved cyst edges produces edge (refraction) shadows, not a duplicated structure.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Side lobe/grating lobe artifacts can create

options.text: False echoes that appear to originate from the main beam path
Multiple equally spaced echoes from parallel reflectors
False Doppler signals but no effect on the grayscale B-mode image
Duplicated structures deep to the diaphragm

explanation: Reduce with apodization; recognize as artifact vs real masses.

distractorExplanations.b: Equally spaced echoes from parallel reflectors are reverberation, not side- or grating-lobe artifact.
distractorExplanations.c: Lobe artifacts affect both B-mode and Doppler, placing off-axis echoes as if they were on the beam axis.
distractorExplanations.d: A duplicated structure deep to the diaphragm is mirror-image artifact, not a lobe artifact.

prompt: The ALARA principle means:

options.text: Use the lowest output possible even if images are nondiagnostic
Use output exposures As Low As Reasonably Achievable
Keep exposure below a fixed legal dose limit per exam
Track cumulative ionizing dose as with CT

explanation: Use output exposures As Low As Reasonably Achievable for diagnostic quality. Monitor MI/TI; reduce power, dwell time, and use appropriate modes.

distractorExplanations.a: ALARA balances exposure against diagnostic quality; a nondiagnostic exam is not reasonable and may need repeating.
distractorExplanations.c: ALARA is a judgment principle, not a per-exam dose limit; diagnostic ultrasound has no ionizing dose to cap.
distractorExplanations.d: Ultrasound is non-ionizing, so there is no cumulative ionizing dose to track as with CT.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Mechanical index (MI) relates most to risk of:

options.text: Heating of fetal bone
Aliasing at high PRF
Cavitation bioeffects
Ionizing DNA damage

explanation: TI relates to heating; MI to mechanical/cavitation; contrast agents raise cavitation concern.

distractorExplanations.a: Bone heating is estimated by the thermal index for bone (TIB), not the mechanical index.
distractorExplanations.b: Aliasing is a Doppler sampling artifact related to low PRF, not a bioeffect indexed by MI.
distractorExplanations.d: Ultrasound is non-ionizing; MI relates to mechanical effects such as cavitation, not ionizing damage.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Thermal index (TI) estimates

options.text: Likelihood of cavitation from peak rarefactional pressure
The exact measured temperature rise in tissue
Cumulative ionizing dose to the fetus
Potential tissue heating from ultrasound absorption

explanation: TIS/TIB/TIC variants depend on assumptions; minimize dwell especially with bone/fetal concerns.

distractorExplanations.a: Cavitation likelihood from peak rarefactional pressure is described by the mechanical index (MI), not TI.
distractorExplanations.b: TI is a modeled ratio of output power to the power needed to raise tissue 1°C, not a measured temperature.
distractorExplanations.c: Ultrasound is non-ionizing; TI estimates heating, not radiation dose.

prompt: Range ambiguity artifact occurs when:

options.text: Echoes from deep structures return after the next pulse is sent
Sound travels slower than the assumed 1540 m/s in tissue
Echoes bounce repeatedly between two strong parallel reflectors
The pulse repetition period is much longer than the echo time

explanation: Range ambiguity occurs when the PRP is too short; reduce it by lowering PRF/scale or adjusting depth/timing expectations.

distractorExplanations.b: A slower actual speed causes a speed (range) error that places reflectors too deep, not range ambiguity.
distractorExplanations.c: Repeated bouncing between parallel reflectors is reverberation artifact.
distractorExplanations.d: A long PRP lets all echoes return before the next pulse, which prevents range ambiguity.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Slice thickness artifact can fill in:

options.text: The spectral window due to turbulent flow
Anechoic structures with false echoes
Acoustic shadows distal to calcifications
Gaps between scan lines in the far field

explanation: False echoes from beam elevation thickness fill in anechoic structures; elevational focusing/1.5D arrays reduce slice thickness artifacts.

distractorExplanations.a: Spectral window fill-in comes from turbulence or a large gate, not from slice thickness.
distractorExplanations.c: Shadows deep to calcifications are attenuation artifacts; slice thickness adds echoes to anechoic areas.
distractorExplanations.d: Gaps between far-field lines relate to line density, not to beam thickness in the elevation plane.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Comet-tail artifact is a form of:

options.text: Mirror imaging across a strong reflector like the diaphragm
Refraction at the edges of curved structures
Reverberation from closely spaced strong reflectors
Propagation speed error from passing through fat

explanation: Comet-tail is a dense reverberation pattern from metal/cholesterol etc.

distractorExplanations.a: A duplicated structure across the diaphragm is mirror-image artifact, not comet tail.
distractorExplanations.b: Refraction at curved edges produces edge shadows, not the tapering echo trail of a comet tail.
distractorExplanations.d: Slower speed in fat causes range errors and displacement, not a dense trail of reverberation echoes.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Range ambiguity artifact can occur when:

options.text: PRF is so high that deep echoes return after the next pulse is sent
PRF is so low that echoes return long before the next pulse is sent
Sound reflects back and forth between two strong parallel interfaces
Sound speed in the tissue is lower than the assumed 1540 m/s

explanation: If listening time is too short, late echoes are mis-mapped to shallow depths.

distractorExplanations.b: A low PRF gives a long listening time, so every echo returns before the next pulse; that prevents range ambiguity.
distractorExplanations.c: Back-and-forth reflection between parallel interfaces is reverberation artifact.
distractorExplanations.d: A lower actual speed causes a range (speed) error that displays reflectors too deep, not range ambiguity.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Which bioeffect is more associated with cavitation risk?

options.text: Only skin burns from the keyboard
Mechanical/nonthermal effects monitored conceptually by MI
Solely the thermal index for bone
MRI projectile risk

explanation: Mechanical index (MI) tracks cavitation risk. Thermal index (TI) tracks heating. Keep both as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA), especially in obstetric imaging.

distractorExplanations.a: Thermal index tracks heating risk, not cavitation; mechanical index (MI) is the cavitation-related parameter.
distractorExplanations.c: Duty factor is the transmit on-time fraction; it feeds heating models more than cavitation risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Frame rate affects how often pulses are sent, a heating/duty-factor issue, not the primary cavitation index.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Edge shadowing (refraction shadow) often appears

options.text: Distal to the edges of a curved structure such as a cyst
Distal to a gallstone with strong central attenuation
Deep to a fluid-filled cyst as a bright band
Proximal to the near wall of a vessel as equally spaced lines

explanation: Edge (refraction) shadowing appears at the curved margins of a cyst or vessel where the beam bends and intensity drops, leaving a thin dark line distal to the edge.

distractorExplanations.b: Shadowing deep to a gallstone is an attenuation shadow from the stone itself, not a refraction edge shadow.
distractorExplanations.c: A bright band deep to a cyst is posterior acoustic enhancement, not edge shadowing.
distractorExplanations.d: Equally spaced lines near a vessel wall are reverberation artifact, not a refraction shadow.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 1). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: To practice ALARA during obstetric ultrasound, a sonographer should

options.text: Use the lowest power setting even when images become nondiagnostic
Minimize output and exposure time while obtaining diagnostic images
Raise output power first, then reduce receiver gain to compensate
Monitor MI only, since heating is not a concern in obstetrics

explanation: ALARA: as low as reasonably achievable exposure consistent with diagnostic needs.

distractorExplanations.a: ALARA still requires diagnostic images; a nondiagnostic scan adds repeat exposure without benefit.
distractorExplanations.c: ALARA calls for increasing receiver gain first and output power only if needed, the reverse order.
distractorExplanations.d: Fetal bone heating makes TI (especially TIB) a key concern in obstetrics, so MI alone is not enough.
